title: Your Models Have Thought Enough: Training Large Reasoning Models to Stop Overthinking
claim: Models rarely produce short outputs unaided, yet truncating reasoning early cuts length sharply while mostly preserving accuracy and sometimes fixing errors.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right: density curve, then two dual-axis bar charts
description: Three side-by-side plots motivate the method. Panel a is a smooth bell-shaped density of token lengths. The mean is marked by a dashed vertical line, and a tiny red-shaded left tail labeled 'Small Proportion' is marked with an arrow, showing short answers are rare. Panel b is a dual-axis grouped bar chart across truncation ratios of 100%, 75%, 50% and 25%. Pink bars show accuracy retention and blue bars show average token length. Blue annotations give the length reductions (-25.9%, -51.6%, -77.5%). Accuracy falls only slowly, from 100% to 92% to 74% to 46%. Panel c has the same layout for wrong answers, with green bars for error correction ratio and blue bars for token length. Error correction stays non-zero and rises at 25%. Bars carry numeric labels, and subpanel captions sit underneath.
caption: a. The token length distribution of 500 answers generated by DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B on a math problem. Answers shorter than 1,000 tokens are extremely rare, showing that LRMS hard to produce short answers on their own. b. The effect of truncation ratios on the Accuracy Retention Ratio and token compression for the DeepSeek-R1-Distil-Qwen-7B model on the MATH500 dataset. c. The effect of truncation ratios on the Error Correction Ratio and token compression for wrong answers.
abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) have achieved impressive performance on challenging tasks, yet their deep reasoning often incurs substantial computational costs. To achieve efficient reasoning, existing reinforcement learning methods still struggle to construct short reasoning path during the rollout stage, limiting effective learning. Inspired by Evidence Accumulation Models, we find that LRMs have accumulated sufficient information early in reasoning, making further reasoning steps redundant. Based on this insight, we propose Just-Enough Thinking (JET), which trains models to proactively terminate unnecessary reasoning. JET performs trajectory truncation during rollout to expose the model to short, distributionally consistent reasoning paths. Besides, it uses a quality-controlled length reward to better encourage concise reasoning while maintaining correctness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that JET significantly improves reasoning efficiency without sacrificing accuracy. Especially, DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B achieves a 4.6% accuracy gain while reducing output length by 46.3% on the Olympiad benchmark. Our code is available in the GitHub.
